title: Mirror Match
description: This is a click-based symmetry puzzle. The 64x64 grid is divided down the center by a vertical line. The left half shows a static reference pattern of colored filled cells. The right half starts empty, and the player clicks cells on the right to paint them, recreating the mirror image of the left pattern. Correctly placed cells turn solid green; incorrect ones flash red and reset to empty. A small counter at the top tracks matched cells vs. total required. The level completes when every mirror cell is correctly filled. Level 1 presents a 3-cell L-shape in a single color so one axis of reflection is clear. Later levels use larger irregular patterns with two colors, then three, requiring the player to track both position and color simultaneously while holding the reflected layout in mind.

title: Signal Chain
description: This is a connect-the-dots routing puzzle. Several target circles are scattered across the 64x64 grid, each marked with a distinct inner symbol such as a dot, bar, triangle, cross, or diamond. Wall tiles are shown as dark filled squares. A small preview strip at the top displays these symbols in the order they must be connected. The player clicks the matching circles in that sequence. When two consecutive correct circles are clicked, a straight colored line segment draws between them if no wall tile blocks the direct path; otherwise the attempt flashes red and that segment is not placed. Clicking a circle out of sequence also gives a brief error flash. Once all circles are linked in the required order, the full chain brightens and the level ends. Level 1 uses three circles with very distinct symbols in a wide open layout so the preview-to-target matching rule is instantly clear. Later levels add more circles and clusters of wall tiles that block some direct connections, forcing the player to read the preview carefully and plan the whole route before committing.

title: Shadow Step
description: This is a trail-avoidance movement puzzle. The player moves a bright square token across the 64x64 grid with WASD to reach a marked exit cell. Every cell the token has visited turns into a faded shadow tile and is permanently blocked for the rest of that level. If the token attempts to re-enter any shadow tile the level resets immediately. No other walls exist. The full trail is always visible as a dim color behind the token so the player can see which paths are still open. Level 1 gives a short straight distance and a wide open field so almost any walk reaches the exit. Later levels pre-place patches of shadow tiles that funnel the player into a specific winding route, or shrink the open area so that naive movement quickly self-traps, making careful path planning the central skill.

title: Frequency Lock
description: This is a step-timed color recognition puzzle. Wide colored bands occupy horizontal lanes and move from right to left across the 64×64 grid, but they advance only when the player presses LEFT or RIGHT. A thin vertical strike line sits near the left side. A target-color indicator shows which band color should be hit. Each LEFT or RIGHT press shifts all bands left by one logical unit and consumes one action budget unit, but does not score. Pressing SPACE does not move the bands; it only attempts a hit at the current state. If a band of the target color overlaps the strike line when SPACE is pressed, that band flashes brighter, the hit counter increases, and that band is removed or marked as already claimed. If SPACE is pressed when no target-colored band is on the strike line, the screen gives brief error feedback and the action is wasted. The level ends when the required number of correct hits is reached. Level 1 uses a single lane, one slow band, and one required hit so the player immediately learns that directional actions advance time and SPACE commits the guess. Later levels add more colors, tighter spacing, and multiple lanes so the player must manage when to advance and when to fire.

title: Gravity Drop
description: This is a side-view column-placement puzzle. The 64x64 grid represents a tall shaft seen from the side, with gravity pointing down. Fixed platform tiles at various heights occupy different columns, visible as solid horizontal bars. A block token waits at the top, and a small cursor arrow indicates which column it will fall through. The player presses LEFT or RIGHT to shift the column cursor and presses SPACE to release the block, which then falls straight down and lands on the highest platform tile in that column, or on the floor if no platform exists. A highlighted target platform marks where the block must land. Level 1 has two columns and one low target platform so a single column choice and one drop is all that is needed. Later levels pack the shaft with more columns and staggered platforms at varying heights, requiring the player to read which column produces the correct landing depth.

title: Conveyor Sort gpt
description: This is a factory-routing puzzle on a 64x64 grid where a small crate starts at an input chute and must be sent into the correct receiving bin by setting visible conveyor splitters. The board should look like a top-down workshop: thick conveyor belts, one chunky crate, one highlighted goal bin, and a few large arrow junctions where the track can branch left or right. Clicking a junction flips its arrow and immediately redraws the outgoing belt direction, so the player always sees the full route before committing. Pressing SPACE releases the crate, which then rides along the belts until it reaches the goal bin or a wrong dead-end bumper. Level 1 should have one obvious junction and one wrong branch so the rule is learned in a single interaction. Later levels should add more splitters, longer belt runs, and cases where two nearby branches can be confused visually, making the challenge about reading and configuring the routing hardware rather than reacting quickly.

title: Shutter Dash gpt
description: This is a timing-and-movement puzzle where the player walks a small runner through a corridor full of shutters that alternate between open and closed every step. The grid should show thick wall blocks, bright door-like shutters, a start pad, and a goal tile, with the shutters clearly changing color and shape when they switch state. The player moves with WASD, and every action advances the shutter cycle by one tick; pressing SPACE causes the player to wait in place for one tick, which is essential once timing matters. Level 1 should use just one shutter in a straight hallway so the player sees that moving and waiting both change the gate state. Later levels should add side alcoves for safe waiting, pairs of shutters with opposite timing, and longer hallways where the correct route depends on syncing movement with the cycle. The difficulty should come from watching and planning around a visible rhythm, not from hidden traps or fast reactions.

title: Counterweight Lift gpt
description: This is a vertical lift puzzle where the player moves a worker through a scaffold tower and adjusts a platform’s height by clicking large counterweight baskets. The board should look like a cross-section of a lift shaft: a central elevator platform, ropes or rails beside it, two chunky weight baskets at the bottom, and an exit door on a ledge higher up. Clicking the left or right basket moves one visible weight block from one side to the other, causing the platform to rise or fall by one clean level. The player uses UP, DOWN, LEFT, and RIGHT to walk on and off the platform, so the core puzzle is to set the lift to the right height and use it to reach useful ledges. Level 1 should show a single ledge one step above the floor, so one click makes the mechanic obvious and the worker can ride directly to the exit area. In later levels, the exit should not be reachable directly from the first lift. Instead, the player must ride to an intermediate ledge, step off, and travel to a different lift station or control point, then change the height of another lift to continue upward. These later levels should use multiple ledges and small wall partitions so that ledges are not decorative resting places but necessary transfer points between lift systems on the way to the exit.

title: Shape Mold gpt
description: This is a movement puzzle where the player controls a soft clay block and must reshape it by passing through cutters until it fits through the exit frame. The board should show a clearly visible clay piece made of several tiles, fixed wall boundaries, a few cutter gates with distinct silhouettes, and a destination outline that visibly matches the required final shape. Moving with WASD pushes the whole clay body one cell at a time; when it passes through a cutter, any part of the clay that overlaps the cutter's blade region is trimmed away immediately. Level 1 should use a very simple block and one obvious cutter so the player instantly understands that the shape can be changed by movement. Later levels should use two or three cutters placed in different corridors, so the player must choose an order that removes the correct protrusions without over-cutting. The core challenge is reading the visible silhouette changes and routing the clay through the right tools, not learning lots of special-case rules.

title: Room Swap gpt
description: This is a rearrangement puzzle where the board is divided into large framed rooms and the player must swap whole rooms to create a walkable path from the start to the exit. The screen should look like a 2x2 or 3x2 set of boxed chambers, each chamber containing its own little walls, floor openings, and sometimes the player or the exit. Clicking one room frame highlights it, and clicking a second room frame swaps the entire contents of those two rooms while keeping the outer board fixed. The player then moves with WASD inside the newly arranged layout, so the game alternates between a big structural edit and small local navigation. Level 1 should require one obvious swap to connect a broken corridor. Later levels should require two or more swaps, with chambers that look similar enough to invite mistakes but still remain fully readable. The mechanic should feel like physically sliding whole puzzle sections into place rather than rotating tiles or guessing hidden states.

title: River Ferry gpt
description: This is a transport puzzle where the player walks along riverbanks and rides a small ferry raft between separated islands to reach a flag. The board should show blue water channels, brown or green land patches, one raft big enough to stand on, and clearly marked dock posts on each shore. The player moves with WASD on land and on the raft, but the raft only travels when the player clicks a large dock bell or lever positioned beside a dock, causing the ferry to cross to its paired dock. Level 1 should have one straight river crossing so the player immediately learns that the raft is the only way over water. Later levels should add two or three docks connected in different ways, so the player must decide which bank to stand on before sending the ferry away. Some levels can place the raft on the wrong side at the start, creating a simple recovery problem that is still completely visible from the opening frame.

title: Echo Maze gpt
description: This is a navigation puzzle where most of the maze is hidden in darkness and the player reveals nearby walls by sending out visible echo pulses. The screen should be mostly dark floor with the player shown as a bright beacon, and walls should appear only when lit by an expanding ring effect from the player's position. The player moves with WASD, and pressing SPACE sends an echo pulse that briefly reveals walls, hazards, and the goal within a circular radius before they fade back into darkness. Level 1 should be a tiny room where one pulse clearly shows the route to the goal, making the reveal mechanic instantly understandable. Later levels should use larger mazes with dead ends and a small limit on how many pulses are available, so the player must remember the revealed structure and move confidently between scans. The game should still avoid cheap guesswork by making the local area around the player always faintly visible, so each pulse extends knowledge rather than replacing all visibility.

title: Mirror Walk gpt
description: This is a dual-control puzzle where the player moves a character on one half of the board while a mirrored twin moves symmetrically on the other half, and both positions matter. The grid should be split by a central divider, with the left and right rooms laid out as reflected spaces containing buttons, walls, and one exit door. Pressing WASD moves the main character normally and the twin in the mirrored direction at the same time, so moving right on the left side makes the twin move left on the right side. Level 1 should simply show that both avatars move together and that either one hitting a wall stays blocked while the other can still move if its path is open. Later levels should place a button under the twin that must be held down while the main character reaches the exit, or use asymmetrical wall differences so the player has to exploit one side getting blocked while the other keeps moving. The first frame should make the symmetry obvious so the challenge is about reasoning over coupled motion, not deciphering the interface.

title: Flood Fill
description: This is a region-painting puzzle on a 64x64 grid divided into irregular solid-color blobs. The player clicks any cell to flood that blob with the current active color, chosen by clicking one of five color swatches drawn as thick square buttons along the bottom edge of the board. The goal is to make the entire board a single uniform color within a target move limit shown as a number at the top. Level 1 presents four large simple blobs in two colors with a generous budget so the flood mechanic is obvious after one or two clicks. Later levels pack in twelve to twenty irregular jagged regions with tight limits that force the player to plan a careful merge order, thinking several steps ahead about which color to spread into which neighbor before committing. The board always reads as a flat quilt of solid patches; clicking any patch recolors it instantly and visually merges it with all touching cells of the same new color. There is no movement, no timing, and no hidden state — the entire puzzle is visible at once and the only challenge is choosing the right sequence of color floods.

title: Shadow Match
description: This is a projection-reasoning puzzle split into two 32x64 half-panels placed side by side. The left panel shows a fixed front-on view of stacked colored square blocks arranged in columns of varying height, like a bar chart made of chunky tiles. The right panel shows a blank same-size grid where the player must recreate the correct top-down shadow silhouette by clicking cells to toggle them between dark and empty. A cell in the shadow should be dark if any block exists anywhere in that column in the front view. A confirm button at the bottom edge turns green when the drawn shadow matches the correct projection or flashes red otherwise. Level 1 presents three or four simple straight columns so the projection rule is grasped immediately. Later levels use L-shaped and staggered block arrangements where multiple column heights create overlapping shadows and some cells that appear occupied from the front cast no top-down shadow at all. The left panel never changes; only the right shadow grid is editable.

title: Wire the Circuit
description: This is a connection puzzle on a 64x64 grid where a power source cell shown as a bright yellow filled square sits near the top of the board and a load cell shown as a bright cyan filled square sits near the bottom. Pre-placed wire segment tiles already cover much of the path between them, drawn as short thick lines that meet at cell edges to form continuous runs. Some segments are missing, shown as visually dark gap cells. The player clicks an empty gap cell to place a wire tile, and clicking the same cell again rotates it ninety degrees through straight-horizontal, straight-vertical, and two corner orientations. When a fully unbroken connected path runs from source to load, the entire wire chain lights up brighter to signal completion. Level 1 has a single straight gap of three cells so the mechanic is clear immediately. Later levels introduce branching dead-end stubs that mislead routing, segments that only complete the path in one specific rotation, and dense layouts where nearly the whole grid is filled with fixed tiles that constrain the valid route to a single solution. Only gap cells respond to clicks; all pre-placed tiles are fixed.

title: Sliding Rows
description: This is a row-alignment puzzle on a 64x64 board divided into horizontal strips, each four cells tall. Every strip contains a row of colored square tiles that slides left or right as a unit when the player clicks that row and presses the left or right arrow key, or clicks and drags. Tiles that slide off one edge reappear on the opposite edge. The goal is to align all rows so that same-color tiles form solid vertical columns running top to bottom across all strips simultaneously. A vertical column of cells all sharing the same color lights up bright white as a reward signal. Level 1 has three strips and two colors with small initial offsets so one or two slides produce alignment. Later levels add up to eight strips with four distinct colors and large randomized offsets where every strip needs independent adjustment and moving one row closer to aligning one column may misalign another. There is no pushing, no tile swapping, and no diagonal movement, making the core challenge purely the coordination of independent horizontal offsets across all rows at once.

title: Echo Step
description: This is a prediction puzzle on a 64x64 open board where the player controls a solid green square token using UP, DOWN, LEFT, and RIGHT. One or two ghost echo tokens follow the player’s movement history with fixed delays: the first echo repeats the move the player made a short time earlier, and the second echo repeats an even older move. All tokens remain visible at all times and update whenever the player takes a movement action. The board contains separate goal zones drawn as dark-bordered rectangles, each decorated with a distinct icon that identifies which token belongs there. One goal zone uses the same filled-square icon as the player token, one uses a ring icon matching the first echo, and one uses a diamond icon matching the second echo. The level is solved only when every token is standing on its matching goal zone at the same time. Level 1 should use a single echo and place the two goal zones close together so the delayed-following relationship becomes obvious within a few moves. Later levels should place the goal zones farther apart and introduce the second echo with a longer delay, requiring the player to predict where all tokens will end up several moves ahead before choosing a direction. The board is otherwise empty, with no walls or obstacles.
